questions.stem: A black square PQRS has been cut into two parts. One part of it is shown in Panel I. Which one of the shapes in Panel II is the other part?
questions.figure: Panel I is the square PQRS (S top left, R top right, P bottom left, Q bottom right) drawn on a 6 by 6 grid of unit cells. Black cells by row from the top (# is black, . is not black): row 1 ######, row 2 #.##.., row 3 #....#, row 4 ###.##, row 5 #...##, row 6 ######. Panel II shows four black shapes, each inside a box 5 cells wide and 4 cells tall (X is black, . is empty), rows from the top: (i) X..XX / XXXX. / ..X.. / XXXX.  (ii) X..XX / XXXX. / ..X.. / .XXX.  (iii) X..XX / XXXX. / ..X.. / XXX..  (iv) X..XX / XXXX. / ..XX. / .XX..

diagram.alt: Square PQRS on a 6 by 6 grid with its black cells, and four black shapes (i) to (iv) each in a 5 by 4 box.

solutionDiagram.alt: The square with the 25 black cells and the 11 light leftover cells, the leftover shape, and options (i) to (iv) with extra and missing cells marked.

options: (ii)
(iii)
(iv)

steps.title: What the question asks and the one rule
steps.body: A square is cut into two parts when a cut splits it into two pieces that together cover it exactly, with no gap and no overlap. So the missing part is whatever is left of the square once the shown piece is removed. The square here is drawn on a grid of unit cells, so a piece is just a set of cells. The one rule: the other part is the square minus the shown part, and it must have exactly that outline. It can be turned or flipped to compare, but never resized, so an option with a different number of cells or a different outline cannot be the other part.

steps.title: Count the black cells
steps.body: Number the rows 1 to 6 from the top and the columns 1 to 6 from the left. Black cells: row 1 has all six, row 2 has columns 1, 3 and 4, row 3 has columns 1 and 6, row 4 has columns 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6, row 5 has columns 1, 5 and 6, and row 6 has all six. That is $6+3+2+5+3+6=25$ black cells. The square has $6\times 6=36$ cells, so the other part has 11 cells.

steps.title: List the cells that are not black
steps.body: Row 2: columns 2, 5, 6. Row 3: columns 2, 3, 4, 5. Row 4: column 4. Row 5: columns 2, 3, 4. That is $3+4+1+3=11$ cells, as counted. They all lie in the box of columns 2 to 6 and rows 2 to 5, which is 5 wide and 4 tall, the same box size as the Panel II shapes. Written as rows of that box (X is a cell of the missing part): X..XX, XXXX., ..X.., XXX..

steps.title: Compare with each option
steps.body: (i) has 4 cells in its bottom row, so it has 12 cells: one too many. (ii) has 11 cells, but its bottom bar is shifted one place to the right (.XXX. instead of XXX..), so it sits under the middle of the stem instead of ending at the stem. (iv) has 11 cells, but its stem is two cells thick and its bottom bar is only two cells long, so the outline differs. (iii) agrees with the missing part in every row: X..XX, XXXX., ..X.., XXX.. . Turning or flipping any other option does not make it equal to the missing part either. Answer: option (iii), which is (C).

shortcut.body: Count the black cells (25), so the missing part has 11 cells; that rejects (i), which has 12. Then look only at the bottom row of the empty region: a bar of three cells whose right end is directly under the one-cell stem, starting at the left edge of the box. Only (iii) has that. About 1.5 minutes. Counting is safe here because the figure sits on a grid; on a free-form figure compare outlines instead.

traps.text: Choosing (i) because its top three rows match. It has one more cell in the bottom bar, and 12 cells cannot fill a hole of 11.
Choosing (ii) because it also has 11 cells and a three-cell bar. The bar must end under the stem and start at the left edge of the box; (ii) shifts it right by one cell.
Choosing (iv) after counting 11 cells. A matching count does not prove a match: its stem is two cells thick and its bar two cells long, unlike the one-cell stem and three-cell bar of the hole.

recognize.clues: Two parts of one square, a shape drawn on a grid of cells, and the words "the other part": the task is to fit pieces together with no gap and no overlap.
recognize.contrast: Not a symmetry or reflection question: the other part is not a mirror image of the shown part. Its outline comes from filling the leftover cells, so counting and matching beats flipping.

check.body: Count by columns instead of rows. The square's black cells per column are 6, 3, 4, 3, 4, 5 (total 25). The chosen shape, read from its own picture, has 3, 2, 3, 2, 1 cells in its five columns, and these sit in columns 2 to 6 of the square. Column by column the totals are 6, 3+3, 4+2, 3+3, 4+2, 5+1, so every column of six cells is exactly full. The total is $25+11=36$, the size of the square.

questions.stem: The figure shows two 4-tile patterns. Either one or both of the patterns can be used any number of times and in any orientation to construct a new pattern. Which one of the options below cannot be constructed by using only these two 4-tile patterns assuming there are no overlaps among them?
questions.figure: Two tile patterns: a 2 by 2 block of four squares, and a straight bar of four squares in a column. Options are black rectangles of unit squares: (A) 4 squares wide and 2 tall, (B) 4 wide and 3 tall, (C) 5 wide and 3 tall, (D) 5 wide and 4 tall.

diagram.alt: The 2 by 2 block and the 1 by 4 bar, then the four rectangular target patterns A to D drawn as grids.

solutionDiagram.alt: Tilings of options A, B and D with the two tile shapes, and option C shown as 15 cells.

options: A 4 by 2 rectangle of squares
A 4 by 3 rectangle of squares
A 5 by 3 rectangle of squares
A 5 by 4 rectangle of squares

steps.title: What is being asked
steps.body: A tile pattern is a group of unit squares stuck edge to edge. Here we have two building pieces: a 2 by 2 block and a 1 by 4 bar. Each piece covers exactly 4 unit squares. To build a bigger shape, pieces must fit with no overlap and no gap. The one rule that decides the question: the number of squares in a built pattern is a whole number of pieces times 4, so it must be a multiple of 4.

steps.title: Count the squares in each option
steps.body: Squares = width times height. Option A: $4 \times 2 = 8$. Option B: $4 \times 3 = 12$. Option C: $5 \times 3 = 15$. Option D: $5 \times 4 = 20$.

steps.title: Show the multiples of 4 really can be built
steps.body: A: two 2 by 2 blocks side by side. B: three horizontal bars stacked, each 4 long. D: five vertical bars of height 4 side by side. These three can be built, so they are not the answer.

steps.title: Option C is impossible
steps.body: 15 is not a multiple of 4, so no collection of whole pieces can cover it. Answer: option (C).

shortcut.body: Count squares in each option and test divisibility by 4. Only 15 fails. This takes about 20 seconds. The test only rules out shapes, so confirm the other three by a quick tiling, as above.

traps.text: Thinking a 4 by 2 rectangle needs a bar: it is just two square blocks.
Believing 3 rows cannot be made from 2 by 2 blocks. Three horizontal bars do it.
Choosing D because 5 columns look odd. Five vertical bars of height 4 tile it exactly.

recognize.clues: Two fixed tile patterns reused any number of times, in any orientation, with no overlap, and a question about what cannot be constructed: this asks for an invariant of the pieces.
recognize.contrast: Not a symmetry question although the tiles look regular. The test is a property of area, not of mirror or rotation, so counting squares settles it quickly.

check.body: Substitute the piece count k into 4k = area for every option. Options A, B and D give k = 2, 3 and 5, and each matches a tiling you can draw. Option C would need k = 3.75 pieces, and a fractional piece does not exist. Equivalently, three pieces cover 12 squares and leave 3 over, which is too few for a fourth piece.

questions.stem: In Panel I of the figure below, the front view and top view of a structure are shown. Which one of the 3D structures shown in Panel II possesses the views shown in Panel I?
questions.figure: Panel I shows two grey views, each on a 3 by 3 grid of squares. Front view: the left column is 3 squares tall and the middle and right columns are 2 squares tall. Lines inside it split it into four faces: the top left square alone; an L-shaped face made of the left column's two lower squares and the bottom square of the middle column; the bottom right square alone; and a rectangle made of the middle and right squares of the second level. Top view: the whole 3 by 3 square except the front right cell. Lines inside it split it into four faces: the left column's back and middle cells as one tall rectangle; the left column's front cell alone; the back row's middle and right cells as one wide rectangle; and an L-shaped face made of the middle row's middle and right cells and the front row's middle cell. Panel II shows four isometric drawings of stacks of unit cubes on a 3 by 3 floor, each seen from the front, right and above, with arrows marking the top view and the front view. Stack heights read from each drawing, listed row by row from the back row to the front row, each row from left to right: (i) 3 2 2 / 3 1 1 / 2 1 1; (ii) 3 2 2 / 3 2 1 / 2 1 0; (iii) 3 3 2 / 3 1 1 / 2 1 0; (iv) 3 2 2 / 3 1 1 / 2 1 0.

diagram.alt: Front view and top view on 3 by 3 grids with their internal lines, and four isometric cube stacks (i) to (iv).

solutionDiagram.alt: The 3 by 3 height map 3 2 2 / 3 1 1 / 2 1 0, the isometric stack it gives, and one line for why each of (i), (ii) and (iii) fails.

options: (ii)
(iii)
(iv)

steps.title: What the two views mean
steps.body: The structure is a pile of unit cubes standing on a 3 by 3 floor. Describe it by a height map: how many cubes are stacked on each floor cell. The front view is what you see looking horizontally from the front: for each column it shows the tallest stack. The top view is what you see looking straight down: it shows which floor cells are covered. A line drawn inside a view is an edge between two faces that are not in one plane. In the top view that means two neighbouring cells whose stacks have different heights. In the front view it means two neighbouring squares whose faces lie at different depths. The rule: find the height map that produces both views, then pick the picture that has that map.

steps.title: Read the top view
steps.body: Number the floor rows 1 (back) to 3 (front) and the columns 1 to 3 from the left. The front right cell (row 3, column 3) is empty, so its height is 0. Cells in one face have equal height, and cells in different faces differ. So the left column's back and middle cells have one common height $a$; the front left cell has height $b$; the back row's middle and right cells have height $c$; and the L-shaped face, the middle row's middle and right cells and the front middle cell, has one common height $d$, with $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ different from their neighbours across the lines.

steps.title: Read the front view and fix the heights
steps.body: The L-shaped face of the front view is one plane, and the front plane is the front row. It covers the left column at levels 1 and 2 and the middle column at level 1. So the front left cell is 2 high and the front middle cell is 1 high: $b=2$, $d=1$. The bottom right square is a separate face: it is the front of the middle row's right cell, one row behind the front plane, and it is 1 high, consistent with $d=1$. The rectangle at level 2 over the middle and right columns is the front of the back row, so $c=2$. The top left square is the front of the tower above the front left cell, and it lies in the middle row: $a=3$. The columns' tallest stacks are then 3, 2, 2, as the front view shows.

steps.title: Check that nothing else fits
steps.body: A script listed every height map with heights 0 to 3 on the 9 cells and kept those whose top view and front view have exactly the faces above. Only the map in the previous step survives, so the structure is fixed and has 15 cubes.

steps.title: Match the options
steps.body: (i) has a block on the front right cell as well (front row 2 1 1), so its top view would be a full square: rejected. (ii) has the middle cell of the right column 2 high while its neighbour is 1 high (middle row 3 2 1), so the L-shaped top face would split: rejected. (iii) has a back middle block 3 high like the tower (back row 3 3 2), so the front view would be 3 high over two columns and the top faces would merge: rejected. (iv) has back row 3 2 2, middle row 3 1 1 and front row 2 1 0, exactly the height map. Answer: option (iv), which is (D).

shortcut.body: Use the top view first. Its front right corner is empty, so reject any picture whose front row has three blocks: that is (i). Then use the equal-height faces: the back row's two right cells are one flat face, and the middle row's two right cells are one flat face. In (iii) the back middle block is as tall as the tower, and in (ii) the middle block of the right column is a step higher than its neighbour. Both break a face, so only (iv) is left. About 3 minutes. The method is safe when no cube is hidden behind another, which is the case in all four drawings.

traps.text: Matching (i) on the front view alone: it also has tallest stacks 3, 2, 2. Its filled front right cell shows only in the top view, which would then be a full square.
Matching (ii) on the outline of both views. Its extra step in the middle of the right column changes only the faces inside the views, so the lines in the top view are what reject it.
Taking (iii) because its tall stack is on the left. Its back middle block is also 3 high, so the front view would show a second column 3 squares tall, not 2.

recognize.clues: A front view and a top view given together, and a choice of 3D stacks: two projections must be matched to one height map.
recognize.contrast: Not a cube-net or dice question. There is no folding; the unknown is how many cubes stand on each cell, found by combining the two flat views.

check.body: Take the height map 3 2 2 / 3 1 1 / 2 1 0 and read it back. Column maxima from left to right are 3, 2, 2, which matches the front view. The only empty cell is the front right one, which matches the top view, and the total is $3+2+2+3+1+1+2+1+0=15$ cubes.

questions.stem: The paper as shown in the figure is folded to make a cube where each square corresponds to a particular face of the cube. Which one of the following options correctly represents the cube? Note: The figures shown are representative.
questions.figure: A net of six squares. A vertical column of three squares holds, from top to bottom: a filled circle, a hollow triangle, a hollow circle. A horizontal row of four squares runs through the middle square of the column: blank, hollow triangle (the column square), blank, filled triangle.

diagram.alt: Cross shaped net: column filled circle, hollow triangle, hollow circle; middle row blank, hollow triangle, blank, filled triangle.

solutionDiagram.alt: Table of the six cube faces and the three pairs of opposite faces.

options: Front face hollow triangle, top face filled circle
Front face hollow triangle, right face filled triangle
Front face hollow triangle, with the visible top and right faces both blank
Front face hollow triangle, top face filled triangle, right face filled circle

steps.title: Definitions and the rule
steps.body: A net is a flat layout that folds into a cube; each square becomes one face. Two faces are opposite when they never touch. In a straight strip of four squares that wraps around the cube, the squares two places apart are opposite. The rule: a cube picture is correct only if no two opposite faces are shown side by side.

steps.title: Find the opposite pairs
steps.body: The horizontal strip blank, hollow triangle, blank, filled triangle wraps around the cube, so hollow triangle is opposite filled triangle and the two blanks are opposite. The remaining column has filled circle above and hollow circle below the hollow triangle, so those two are opposite.

steps.title: Test each option
steps.body: (A) shows hollow triangle and filled circle adjacent: allowed, since the circle sits on the face above the triangle in the net. (B) puts filled triangle next to hollow triangle: they are opposite, impossible. (C) puts two blank faces side by side: they are opposite, impossible, and the top face must hold the circle. (D) puts the filled triangle on top and the filled circle on the right next to hollow triangle: filled triangle is opposite hollow triangle, impossible. Answer: option (A).

shortcut.body: Write the three opposite pairs from the net (about 30 seconds), then discard any picture that shows an opposite pair on two visible faces. Options B, C and D each show one.

traps.text: Putting the filled triangle on the side of the hollow triangle because they sit in the same row in the net. In a four-square strip the squares two places apart are opposite; here the hollow and filled triangles are two apart, so they cannot both be visible.
Forgetting that the two blank squares flank the hollow triangle on opposite sides, so they can never both be visible with it.
Mixing up which face carries the circle: the circle faces are above and below the hollow triangle, and the filled triangle is behind it.

recognize.clues: A flat paper of six squares with a symbol on each, folded into a cube, with options showing three visible faces: this is a net-to-cube question.
recognize.contrast: Not a dice question. Dice problems give a rule such as opposite faces summing to 7; here the opposite pairs must be derived from the shape of the net itself.

check.body: The three opposite pairs must use each of the six faces exactly once: hollow and filled triangle, filled and hollow circle, and the two blanks. Squares that share an edge in the net must be neighbours on the cube. The hollow triangle shares edges with both blanks, the filled circle and the hollow circle, and none of these is its partner (the filled triangle), so the pairing is consistent.

questions.stem: A square paper, shown in figure (I), is folded along the dotted lines as shown in the figures (II) and (III). Then a few cuts are made as shown in figure (IV). Which one of the following patterns will be obtained when the paper is unfolded? Note: The figures shown are representative.
questions.figure: Figure I is a plain square. Figure II shows the square folded along a diagonal (dotted line) into a right triangle. Figure III shows that triangle folded along the line from its right-angle corner to the midpoint of its long side, giving a smaller right triangle drawn with its long side on top and its right angle at the bottom. Figure IV shows three cuts: a small filled triangle at the middle of the long top edge with its point towards that edge, a small right triangle on the left short edge, with a flat top, a vertical right side and its long side lying along the slanted edge, and a short horizontal bar touching the right short edge. The four options are unfolded squares with a small triangle at each edge midpoint, plus four marks near the corners; (A) has outward-pointing triangles on all four edges, squares at top-left and bottom-right and L shapes at top-right and bottom-left; (B) has diamonds instead of squares; (C) has the top and bottom triangles pointing inward; (D) has a square at the centre and only two L shapes.

diagram.alt: Four panels: plain square, square folded on a diagonal, folded again on the altitude, and the final small triangle with three cuts.

solutionDiagram.alt: Unfolded square with dashed diagonal creases, four edge triangles, two squares on one diagonal and two L shapes on the other.

options: Outward triangles at all four edge midpoints, squares at top-left and bottom-right, L shapes at top-right and bottom-left
Outward triangles at all four edge midpoints, diamonds at top-left and bottom-right, L shapes at top-right and bottom-left
Top and bottom triangles pointing inward, left and right outward, squares at top-left and bottom-right, L shapes at the other two corners
Outward triangles at all four edge midpoints, one square at the centre, L shapes at top-right and bottom-left only

steps.title: What folding and unfolding means
steps.body: Each fold lays one half of the paper on the other, mirror-fashion. A hole cut through all layers appears once per layer. When you unfold, every cut is copied by reflection in each crease you open. The rule: undo the folds in reverse order and reflect the cut across each crease line.

steps.title: Layers in the final shape
steps.body: Two folds give 4 layers. The long top edge of figure IV is the original paper edge (top and right edges, laid together). The two short sides are creases: one is the first diagonal crease, the other the second fold line, which lies on the other diagonal of the square.

steps.title: Triangle cut on the long edge
steps.body: The long edge is the paper boundary, so the triangle cut sits at an edge midpoint with its point towards the edge. Unfolding reflects it to all four edge midpoints, each with its point towards the edge, that is outward. That removes option (C), whose top and bottom triangles point inward.

steps.title: Cuts touching the creases
steps.body: A cut that touches a crease unfolds into a pair, mirrored in the crease. The left cut is a right triangle whose long side lies on the crease and whose two short sides are horizontal and vertical. Its mirror image in that crease is the same triangle turned over, and the pair together fills an axis-parallel square, not a diamond: this removes option (B). A horizontal bar touching the other diagonal mirrors into a vertical bar joined at its end, an L shape. Each of these appears at two opposite corners, so the pattern has squares at one diagonal and L shapes at the other. Option (D) has a square at the centre, but the triangle cut is away from the centre point, so it is repeated at four places and never lands at the centre. Answer: option (A).

shortcut.body: Use three quick checks in about 2 minutes. Triangles on the boundary point outward. A right triangle with its long side on a 45 degree crease unfolds, with its mirror image, into an axis-parallel square. A cut not at the paper centre never unfolds to a centred mark. Together they leave only (A).

traps.text: Drawing a diamond because the crease is diagonal. The cut triangle has horizontal and vertical short sides, and reflecting it in its long side completes a square with horizontal and vertical sides; a diamond would need short sides at 45 degrees.
Reflecting the edge triangle the wrong way for the top and bottom. An edge cut reflects with its point still towards the paper edge.
Placing the square at the centre, where all four layers meet. The cut is away from that point and so is repeated four times, not once.

recognize.clues: A square folded twice along dotted lines and then cut, with the question asking what is seen after unfolding: fold, cut, unfold by reflection.
recognize.contrast: Not a crease-pattern question. Here the folds are given and the cuts are the unknown; a crease-pattern question runs the other way and asks which folds a given marking came from.

check.body: Count the marks instead of reflecting one. The folded paper has 4 layers. The edge triangle lies wholly inside the paper, so it is cut in all 4 layers and appears 4 times, once per edge midpoint. The left cut and the bar both touch a crease, and a cut on a crease joins two layers into one shape, so each appears twice, not four times: 2 squares on one diagonal and 2 L shapes on the other. That is 4 triangles, 2 squares and 2 L shapes, which fits (A) and rules out (D), with only two L shapes and a centre square. It does not separate (A) from (B); the shape of the joined pair, taken from the reflection step, does that.

The two holes nearest the top edge are 2 cm and 8 cm from the left edge, so they are $8-2=6$ cm apart. The value 4 cm adds the two 2 cm offsets instead of taking them from the 10 cm width, 2 holes ignores the second fold, and 8 cm measures from the wrong edge.

questions.stem: A cube is to be cut into 8 pieces of equal size and shape. Here, each cut should be straight and it should not stop till it reaches the other end of the cube. The minimum number of such cuts required is

solutionDiagram.alt: Two cube faces with dashed lines showing one cut per axis.

steps.title: What a full cut does
steps.body: A straight cut that runs from one end of the cube to the other is a plane through the whole cube. Each such cut splits every piece it passes through into two. With no rearranging between cuts, one plane can at most double the number of pieces, so $k$ cuts give at most $2^k$ pieces.

steps.title: Lower bound
steps.body: We need 8 pieces, so $2^k \ge 8$, which gives $k \ge 3$. Two cuts give at most 4 pieces.

steps.title: Three cuts suffice
steps.body: Cut once through the middle in each of the three directions (left-right, front-back, top-bottom). This gives $2\times2\times2 = 8$ small cubes, all equal in size and shape. Answer: option (A), 3.

shortcut.body: Each plane doubles the count at most, and $2^3 = 8$. Pick 3 at once, about 30 seconds. The doubling bound assumes pieces stay in place between cuts, which is the intended reading.

traps.text: Taking 4 cuts as 8 pieces from 4 faces. Cuts are planes, and three planes in three directions already give 8.
Using the formula for cutting a line of 8 units: 7 cuts. That counts cuts of one line, not planes in three dimensions.
One cut per piece. A single plane makes two pieces, so this wildly overcounts.

recognize.clues: A cube cut by full planes into a required number of equal pieces, with the minimum number of cuts asked for: the block-cutting count of pieces against cuts.
recognize.contrast: Not a faces-edges-vertices count. Euler's formula relates the parts of one polyhedron, while this question counts how many pieces a set of planes can produce.

check.body: Use the block-cutting count instead: $p$, $q$ and $r$ cuts parallel to the three pairs of faces give $(p+1)(q+1)(r+1)$ pieces. With $p+q+r=2$ the most is $2\cdot2\cdot1=4$, below 8, while $p=q=r=1$ gives $2\cdot2\cdot2=8$ equal cubes.

questions.stem: A rectangular paper of 20 cm × 8 cm is folded 3 times. Each fold is made along the line of symmetry, which is perpendicular to its long edge. The perimeter of the final folded sheet (in cm) is

solutionDiagram.alt: Rectangles 20 by 8, 10 by 8, 5 by 8 and 5 by 4 showing each fold.

steps.title: Line of symmetry and perimeter
steps.body: A line of symmetry of a rectangle perpendicular to a long edge cuts that edge into two equal halves; folding on it halves the length of that edge and leaves the other side unchanged. The perimeter of a rectangle $a \times b$ is $2(a+b)$. The key point: after each fold, the long edge may change, so recheck which side is long before the next fold.

steps.title: Fold one
steps.body: The long edge is 20, so halve it: the sheet is $10 \times 8$.

steps.title: Fold two
steps.body: The long edge is still 10, so halve it: $5 \times 8$.

steps.title: Fold three and the perimeter
steps.body: Now 8 is the long edge, so the third fold halves 8: $5 \times 4$. The perimeter is the following. Answer: option (A), 18.

shortcut.body: Track the pair (length, width), always halving the larger side: (20,8), (10,8), (5,8), (5,4). Perimeter 18. About 1 minute. Unsafe only if you forget to recompare the sides.

traps.text: 24 is the perimeter of an 8 by 4 sheet. Reaching it needs the 20 cm side cut down to 4, which halving three times cannot do.
20 is the perimeter of a 5 by 5 sheet. It needs the 8 cm side to shrink to 5, but a fold only halves a side.
Halving the 20 cm side three times gives 2.5 by 8, perimeter 21. After two folds the 8 cm side is the long one, so the third fold must halve that.

recognize.clues: A rectangle folded repeatedly along a line of symmetry and a measurement of the folded sheet: fold-by-fold bookkeeping of the sides.
recognize.contrast: Not a punch-and-unfold question. No cut is made; only the outline of the folded stack is asked, so tracking side lengths replaces reflecting a pattern.

check.body: Every fold halves one side, so the final sheet is $20/2^a$ by $8/2^b$ with $a+b=3$. The four possibilities have perimeters 42 (20 by 1), 24 (10 by 2), 18 (5 by 4) and 21 (2.5 by 8). The rule halve the longer side picks the pair: after 20 becomes 10 and then 5, the side 8 is now the longer one, so the third fold halves 8 and not 5. The 2.5 by 8 sheet would need all three folds on the 20 side, which the rule forbids.

questions.stem: The least number of squares to be added in the figure to make AB a line of symmetry is
questions.figure: A horizontal dashed line AB. Squares of equal size sit against it: one square above the line directly over column 1; below the line, in the first row, squares in columns 0 and 1; in the second row below, one square in column 1. Further right, below the line, in the first row squares in columns 3 and 4, and in the second row one square in column 4. Column 2 is empty.

diagram.alt: Dashed line AB with seven unit squares: one above, six below.

solutionDiagram.alt: The same figure with five extra grey squares above the line mirroring the squares below.

questions.keyNote: The official key is A (6). A direct count gives 5: the mirror of the six squares below is six cells above the line, and one of them (column 1, row 1) already holds a square. The GATE Overflow selected answer also counts 5 and cites option C; the commenters who say 6 do not credit the existing square.

steps.title: Line of symmetry
steps.body: A line AB is a line of symmetry of a figure when the mirror image of the figure in AB is the figure itself. For a grid of squares: for every filled cell, the cell at the same distance on the other side of AB, in the same column, must also be filled.

steps.title: List the filled cells
steps.body: Take row 0 and row 1 below AB, and row -1 and -2 above. Filled cells are (column, row): above (1,-1); below (0,0), (1,0), (1,1), (3,0), (4,0), (4,1). That is 7 cells.

steps.title: Mirror them
steps.body: The mirror of row $r$ is row $-1-r$. The mirrors of the below cells are (0,-1), (1,-1), (1,-2), (3,-1), (4,-1), (4,-2). The mirror of the above cell (1,-1) is (1,0), which is already filled.

steps.title: Count what is missing
steps.body: Of the six required cells above AB, only (1,-1) already exists. So 5 squares are missing: (0,-1), (1,-2), (3,-1), (4,-1), (4,-2). Nothing below needs adding. The count is 5, option (C).

shortcut.body: Count squares on each side: 6 below, 1 above. The 1 above already pairs with a square below, so the needed number is $6 - 1 = 5$. About 1 minute.

traps.text: Adding a full mirror of all 6 lower squares and forgetting the square above AB already matches one of them. This is the official key.
Counting only the squares in the left cluster plus one, ignoring the right cluster below the line.
Mirroring all 7 squares as if none existed on the other side, which double-counts the matched pair.

recognize.clues: A dashed line AB named as a line of symmetry, a set of squares on both sides, and a request for the least number of squares to add: complete the figure by mirror pairs.
recognize.contrast: Not a mirror-image or water-image question. Nothing is flipped to make a new picture; the figure itself must be completed until it equals its own reflection.

check.body: Count by positions instead of by cells. Each distinct mirrored position needs two squares in the final figure, one on each side. Count the distinct positions in the figure, double it, and subtract the squares already drawn; this must agree with the count of empty twins. A square whose twin is present is counted once as a position, not twice.

questions.stem: Looking at the surface of a smooth 3-dimensional object from the outside, which one of the following options is TRUE?
options: The surface of the object must be concave everywhere.
The surface of the object must be convex everywhere.
The surface of the object may be concave in some places and convex in other places.
The object can have edges, but no corners.

steps.title: Words
steps.body: Seen from the outside, a surface is convex at a spot if it bulges towards you, like the outside of a ball, and concave if it dips away from you, like the inside of a bowl. A smooth surface has no edges and no corners: it has a tangent plane at every point. The rule: smooth restricts sharp features, not the pattern of bulges and dips.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.body: A smooth torus (doughnut) bulges on its outer rim and dips on the inner ring hole side, so it has both kinds of region. That shows a smooth object may be convex in some places and concave in others, so (C) is true, and (A) and (B), which say it must be one kind everywhere, are false. A smooth object has no edges, so (D) is false. Answer: option (C).

shortcut.body: Test with one smooth shape that has a dent: a torus or a dimpled ball. It breaks A, B and D at once. About 30 seconds.

traps.text: Reading concave as the default for the outside of a hollow object. From the outside, a ball bulges, so it is convex.
Assuming smooth means round like a ball. Smooth surfaces such as a torus or a peanut shape have dips.
Thinking smooth only bans corners. It also bans edges, since an edge is a crease.

recognize.clues: The words smooth, three-dimensional and from the outside, with options about concave, convex, edges and corners: a question on the local shape of a surface, settled by testing one solid.
recognize.contrast: Not a count of faces, edges and vertices of a polyhedron (ga-spatial.polyhedra-euler): there edges and corners exist, while here the word smooth removes them.

check.body: Second route with a different solid: a golf ball with one soft dent has no crease anywhere, yet it bulges over most of its surface and dips at the dent. It breaks the must-be-concave, must-be-convex and edges-allowed options together, and agrees with the torus used in the solution.

questions.stem: Which one of the options best describes the transformation of the 2-dimensional figure P to Q, and then to R, as shown?
questions.figure: Three five-pointed stars drawn with one long spike. P: long spike points up and to the right. Operation 1 takes P to Q: the long spike now points down and to the right. Operation 2 takes Q to R: the long spike points up and to the right again, and the rest of the star is the up-down mirror of Q.

diagram.alt: Star P, arrow Operation 1 to star Q, arrow Operation 2 to star R.

solutionDiagram.alt: Text trace of the long spike direction: NE, then SE after clockwise rotation, then NE after horizontal reflection.

options: Operation 1: A clockwise rotation by 90° about an axis perpendicular to the plane of the figure. Operation 2: A reflection along a horizontal line
Operation 1: A counter clockwise rotation by 90° about an axis perpendicular to the plane of the figure. Operation 2: A reflection along a horizontal line
Operation 1: A clockwise rotation by 90° about an axis perpendicular to the plane of the figure. Operation 2: A reflection along a vertical line
Operation 1: A counter clockwise rotation by 180° about an axis perpendicular to the plane of the figure. Operation 2: A reflection along a vertical line

steps.title: The operations
steps.body: A rotation turns the figure about a point and keeps its handedness. A reflection in a line flips it to its mirror image: reflection along a horizontal line swaps up and down, reflection along a vertical line swaps left and right. Trace one marked feature, the long spike, through each operation.

steps.title: Operation 1
steps.body: The long spike goes from pointing up-right (NE) to pointing down-right (SE). Turning 90 degrees clockwise takes NE to SE. A counter-clockwise quarter turn would give NW, and a half turn would give SW. In coordinates with $y$ down, clockwise 90 degrees maps $(x,y)\to(-y,x)$: the spike vector $(205,-128)$ becomes $(128,205)$, down-right, as drawn in Q.

steps.title: Operation 2
steps.body: From SE to NE swaps up and down only, which is a reflection along a horizontal line: $(x,y)\mapsto(x,-y)$. A vertical-line reflection would send SE to SW. Answer: option (A).

shortcut.body: Follow only the long spike: NE, then SE, then NE. NE to SE is a clockwise quarter turn, SE to NE is an up-down flip. About 1 minute.

traps.text: Reading the quarter turn as counter-clockwise. That would send NE to NW, not SE.
Choosing a vertical-line reflection for the second step. That flips left and right, sending SE to SW, but R shows NE.
A half turn sends NE to SW, not SE, and a vertical reflection would then give SE, not NE, so both steps fail.

recognize.clues: Two operations applied in a row, P to Q and then Q to R, and options that each name a rotation or a reflection with its axis or line: identify each step and keep the order.
recognize.contrast: A single spike direction cannot tell a rotation from a reflection, since north-east to south-east is either a clockwise quarter turn or a flip in a horizontal line. The mirror-image statement about R and the choices in the options settle which one is meant.

check.body: Compose the two maps with $y$ pointing down: the quarter turn gives $(x,y)\mapsto(-y,x)$ and the flip gives $(x,y)\mapsto(x,-y)$, so together $(x,y)\mapsto(-y,-x)$. The spike $(205,-128)$ goes to $(128,-205)$, which is again up and to the right as drawn in R, and the net map is a reflection, matching R being a mirror image of P.

questions.stem: A palindrome is a word that reads the same forwards and backwards. In a game of words, a player has the following two plates painted with letters. From the additional plates given in the options, which one of the combinations of additional plates would allow the player to construct a five-letter palindrome. The player should use all the five plates exactly once. The plates can be rotated in their plane.
questions.figure: Two plates: A and D. Each option lists three more plates. (A) D, a mirrored D, J. (B) R, an upside-down A, an upside-down R. (C) Z, a mirrored E, D. (D) I, an upside-down L, Y. Every turned plate is its letter rotated through 180 degrees; the D and E look mirrored only because those letters are symmetric top to bottom.

diagram.alt: Plates A and D, then four rows of three plates for options A to D, each turned plate drawn as in the paper.

options: D, a mirrored D, J
R, an upside-down A, an upside-down R
Z, a mirrored E, D
I, an upside-down L, Y

steps.title: Palindrome rule
steps.body: A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards. In a word of 5 letters the 1st and 5th letters match, the 2nd and 4th match, and the 3rd is free. So the letters can be paired off, with exactly one letter left over for the middle. The rule: exactly one letter occurs an odd number of times and every other letter an even number of times. The stem lets plates rotate in their plane, so a plate turned upside down is still its letter; here every turned plate is a letter rotated through 180 degrees, and D and E merely look mirrored.

steps.title: Read each plate as a letter
steps.body: Given: A, D. Option A adds D, D, J: letters A, D, D, D, J. Option B adds R, A, R: letters A, D, R, A, R. Option C adds Z, E, D: letters A, D, Z, E, D. Option D adds I, L, Y: letters A, D, I, L, Y.

steps.title: Count the odd letters
steps.body: A: A, J and D (3 times) are odd, 3 odd letters. B: D once, A twice, R twice, exactly one odd letter. C: A, Z, E odd, 3. D: all five once, 5 odd.

steps.title: Build the word
steps.body: Only B works: the middle plate is D, with A and R on both sides: R A D A R. Answer: option (B).

shortcut.body: Count letters: a 5-letter palindrome needs two pairs and one single. Option B gives A, A, R, R and D. About 1 minute. Unsafe if you read a turned plate as a different letter; B only works when the upside-down R counts as R.

traps.text: Seeing D three times and stopping. A and J stay single, so two odd letters beyond the middle remain.
Matching the mirrored E to nothing. Z, E, A each appear once, so no palindrome forms.
Choosing letters that look symmetric like I and Y. A palindrome needs repeated letters, not symmetric glyphs.

recognize.clues: Plates that may be rotated in their plane, so a plate turned upside down is still the same letter, and the goal is a five-letter word that reads the same forwards and backwards.
recognize.contrast: Not a mirror-image question (ga-spatial.mirror-water-images): a turn through 180 degrees keeps the letter, and the D and E that look mirrored are symmetric letters. Once each glyph is read as a letter the task is a counting problem.

check.body: Independent test on the other options: a five-letter palindrome has four letters in matched pairs, so at most one letter is left without a partner. Options A and C leave three letters unpaired and option D leaves five, so no order of those plates can work.

questions.stem: A plot of land must be divided between four families. They want their individual plots to be similar in shape, not necessarily equal in area. The land has equally spaced poles, marked as dots in the below figure. Two ropes, R1 and R2, are already present and cannot be moved. What is the least number of additional straight ropes needed to create the desired plots? A single rope can pass through three poles that are aligned in a straight line.
questions.figure: Poles form a 7 by 7 lattice with columns 0 to 6 and rows 0 to 6 (row 0 at the top). The two opposite corners, top-right (6,0) and bottom-left (0,6), are missing: the boundary cuts diagonally from (5,0) to (6,1) and from (0,5) to (1,6). Rope R2 is vertical from pole (4,0) down to (4,2). Rope R1 is horizontal from pole (0,4) to (2,4). Each rope covers three poles.

diagram.alt: Lattice of poles with the corner-cut boundary, R2 vertical at the top and R1 horizontal at the left.

solutionDiagram.alt: The land split by three red ropes into two large and two small pentagons, each a square with one corner cut.

steps.title: Similar shapes
steps.body: Two shapes are similar when one is the other scaled up or down, with the same angles and the same ratio between corresponding sides. The plots need not have equal areas, so a big and a small copy of one shape are allowed. Rule: every plot must be a scaled copy of one shape.

steps.title: A target shape
steps.body: The land has two diagonal cuts at opposite corners. A square with one corner cut off (a pentagon) fits the boundary naturally. Two such pieces can be big, with a 4 by 4 square and a cut of legs 2, and two small, with a 2 by 2 square and a cut of legs 1, since scale factor 2 relates them.

steps.title: The three ropes
steps.body: Add the vertical rope from (2,4) to (2,6), the diagonal rope from (2,4) to (4,2) and the horizontal rope from (4,2) to (6,2). With R1 and R2 these cut the land into four pieces: top-left big (4 by 4 minus a triangle of legs 2, area 14), bottom-left small (2 by 2 with corner cut, area 3.5), top-right small (area 3.5) and bottom-right big (area 14). Every piece is a square with one corner cut, and the big ones are twice the small ones.

steps.title: Fewer is impossible
steps.body: An exhaustive search over every rope joining up to three aligned poles finds no way to get four similar plots with 0, 1 or 2 added ropes. So the least number is 3, option (D).

shortcut.body: R1 and R2 each start at the edge and aim at the middle, so the plan is a pinwheel with two diagonal-cut corners as the small pieces. Three ropes complete it; fewer cannot separate four plots. About 3 minutes; in the exam, look for one rope to the bottom edge, one diagonal and one to the right edge.

traps.text: Two more ropes give only three or four regions of unequal shape. Each new rope that reaches the boundary adds one region at most, and the regions would not be similar.
Using one rope per side of the land. Three ropes already meet all four requirements, so four is not minimal.
Adding ropes until every piece has equal area. The question only asks for similar shape, so a 14 and a 3.5 area piece are fine.

recognize.clues: Land on a lattice of poles divided into four plots, with two fixed ropes, the condition similar in shape but not equal in area, and a request for the fewest extra straight ropes: a dissection into scaled copies of one shape.
recognize.contrast: Not a symmetry question (ga-spatial.symmetry): the plots need not be mirror or rotated copies of one another, only scaled copies. Equal area is the look-alike condition; it is stricter than what the question asks.

check.body: Area check on the construction: the land is a 6 by 6 square with two corner triangles of area $0.5$ removed, so its area is $35$. The four plots have areas $14$, $3.5$, $3.5$ and $14$, which also sum to $35$, and the big to small ratio is $4$, the square of the scale factor $2$.

questions.stem: A transparent square sheet shown above is folded along the dotted line. The folded sheet will look like ________.
questions.figure: A transparent square sheet with a vertical dotted fold line through its middle. Two curves meet at a peak on the fold line. On the left half a curve rises from the left edge up to the peak, and two short vertical ticks stand on it, above the curve. On the right half a curve falls from the peak down to the right edge, and two short horizontal ticks hang to the left of it, under the curve. Each option shows the right half as a tall rectangle with the folded-over left half outlined by dashes beside it. (A) Two curves leave the fold at one point and run apart: the upper rises to the right with two vertical ticks above it, the lower falls with two horizontal ticks under it. (B) A closed lens-shaped region between two curves, with two vertical ticks standing up from its lower edge and two horizontal ticks hanging from its upper edge, each vertical tick meeting a horizontal tick in a step. (C) A closed lens with two horizontal lines drawn across it and no vertical ticks. (D) A closed lens with two short step marks hanging from its upper edge, each a vertical tick going down and then a horizontal tick going left.

diagram.alt: Square sheet with a rising curve and two vertical ticks on the left, a falling curve and two horizontal ticks on the right, and four folded-sheet options A to D.

solutionDiagram.alt: The sheet with an arrow showing the left half mirrored over the fold, and the folded sheet as a lens with ticks inside.

options: Two curves running apart from the fold point; the upper one rises to the right with two vertical ticks above it, the lower one falls with two horizontal ticks under it
A lens between two curves, with two vertical ticks standing on the lower edge and two horizontal ticks hanging from the upper edge, each vertical tick meeting a horizontal tick
A lens between two curves with two horizontal lines across it and no vertical ticks
A lens between two curves with two step marks hanging from the upper edge, each a vertical tick going down then a horizontal tick going left

steps.title: What a fold does and the rule
steps.body: Folding along a line turns one half of the sheet over onto the other half. A point at distance $d$ to the left of the fold line lands at distance $d$ to the right of it, at the same height: the left half arrives as its mirror image in the fold line. The sheet is transparent, so both layers show. The folded picture is therefore the right half as it is, drawn together with the mirror image of the left half. The rule: reflect the left half in the fold line only. Do not slide it, flip it upside down, or rotate it.

steps.title: Mirror the left curve
steps.body: Going left to right, the left curve rises to the peak on the fold line. Its mirror image starts at the peak and falls away to the right, steeply at first and then flatter. The right curve also starts at the peak and falls, but slowly at first and then more steeply. Measured on the figure, the left curve ends 122 units below the peak at the outer edge and the right curve ends 125 units below the peak, so after folding the two curves leave the same peak and finish at nearly the same point on the right edge. They enclose a thin lens. The right curve bulges upward, so it is the upper edge, and the mirrored left curve is the lower edge.

steps.title: Place the ticks
steps.body: The two vertical ticks stand on the left curve, above it. A mirror in a vertical line keeps vertical ticks vertical and keeps above as above, so they stand on the lower edge of the lens and point up into it. They land at 55 and 85 units from the fold. The two horizontal ticks hang to the left of the right curve, under it, so they hang from the upper edge and point back towards the fold; they cover 44 to 87 units and 77 to 117 units from the fold. Each vertical tick rises until it meets a horizontal one: the tick at 55 units reaches the first horizontal tick and the tick at 85 reaches the second. The inside of the lens shows two steps.

steps.title: Compare with the options
steps.body: (A) shows the curves running apart, which would need the left curve to rise away from the fold; a mirror makes it fall away, so the curves close into a lens. (C) has no vertical ticks, but a transparent sheet keeps every mark. (D) is a lens, but it hangs the vertical ticks from the upper edge; they belong on the lower edge. (B) has the lens, the vertical ticks standing on the lower edge, the horizontal ticks hanging from the upper edge, and the steps where they meet. Answer: option (B).

shortcut.body: Mirror only the left curve: it must fall away from the fold, so the two curves close into a lens, which removes (A). Then follow one vertical tick. It stays vertical and still stands on the curve that came from the left, which is now the lower edge. (C) has no vertical ticks and (D) hangs them from the upper edge. About 1.5 minutes. The shortcut is safe only because the sheet is transparent; an opaque sheet would hide the lower layer.

traps.text: Choosing (A) by copying the left half to the right without mirroring it. The curve then still rises away from the fold; a fold in a vertical line makes the left curve fall away from the peak.
Choosing (C) because only the horizontal ticks are easy to track. The vertical ticks of the left half do not disappear on a transparent sheet; they stand inside the lens.
Choosing (D) after seeing the lens. It hangs the vertical ticks from the upper edge, but they stood above their curve, and the mirror image of above is still above, so they stand on the lower edge.

recognize.clues: A transparent sheet folded once along a dotted line, with curves and ticks on both halves: every mark of the folded half must be tracked through one mirror fold, and both layers stay visible.
recognize.contrast: A plain reflection (ga-spatial.reflection) shows only the image of a figure. A fold on a transparent sheet shows the original half and the image together, so the picture can close into a lens.

check.body: Unfold test on the chosen picture: reflect its lower edge and its vertical ticks back to the left of the fold. The lower edge becomes a curve rising to the peak with the two vertical ticks above it, which is exactly the left half of the sheet. A picture that does not unfold into the given left half cannot be the folded sheet.

variation.stem: A transparent square sheet is 8 units wide, with its lower-left corner at $(0,0)$. It is folded along the vertical line $x=4$ so that the left half lies over the right half. questions.stem: A polygon is convex if, for every pair of points, P and Q belonging to the polygon, the line segment PQ lies completely inside or on the polygon. Which one of the following is NOT a convex polygon?
questions.figure: Four filled polygons. (A) an arrow-head or chevron shape: a pentagon pointing right with a notch cut into its left side. (B) a triangle. (C) a square. (D) a trapezium with the shorter side on top.

diagram.alt: Four grey polygons: chevron, triangle, square and trapezium.

options: A chevron (arrow-head) shape with a notch on its left side
A triangle
A square
A trapezium

steps.title: Convex test
steps.body: A polygon is convex when no inside angle is greater than 180 degrees. Equivalent test from the question: pick any two points of the shape; if the segment joining them ever leaves the shape, it is not convex. A notch dented into the boundary is exactly such a reflex angle.

steps.title: Check the shapes
steps.body: A triangle, a square and a trapezium have all inside angles below 180 degrees, so each is convex. The chevron has a notch on its left side: the inward vertex has an inside angle above 180 degrees, and a segment joining the two left points on either side of the notch passes outside the shape. So the chevron is not convex. Answer: option (A).

shortcut.body: Scan for a dent. Only the chevron has an inward corner. About 15 seconds.

traps.text: Thinking the pointed triangle is concave because it has sharp tips. Sharp outward corners are still less than 180 degrees.
Doubting the square: all angles are 90 degrees and every segment stays inside.
Reading the slanted sides of the trapezium as a dent. They lean outward, so the angles stay below 180 degrees.

recognize.clues: The question defines convex by the segment PQ staying inside the polygon and asks which of four plain outlines is NOT convex, so only a dent or notch in the outline can make a shape fail.
recognize.contrast: Several of these shapes have mirror lines, but symmetry does not decide convexity. A chevron can be perfectly symmetric and still not convex, because the test is about inward corners.

check.body: Second route by turning direction: walk round the triangle, the square and the trapezium and the outline turns the same way at every corner. Walking round the chevron, it turns the opposite way at the notch corner, and that single reversal is what marks a shape as not convex.

A dent in an outline is an inward corner, where the inside angle opens past a straight line.
A segment joining two boundary points on either side of an inward corner runs outside the shape, which breaks the definition given in the question.
Walk around each shape and look at every corner. Ask whether the outline turns the same way, left or right, at every corner.
A sharp outward tip, such as the corner of a triangle, has a small inside angle and never breaks convexity. Look only for a corner that points into the shape.

variation.stem: Which one of the following polygons, given by the vertices in order around the boundary, is NOT convex? A segment between two points of a convex polygon lies inside or on it.
variation.explanation: Compute the cross product of consecutive edges at each vertex. In the third polygon the vertex $(2,1)$ turns the opposite way to the others, so its inside angle is above 180 degrees and the segment from $(4,3)$ to $(0,3)$ leaves the shape through the dent. The second polygon has the extra vertex $(2,0)$ on a straight edge, an angle of exactly 180 degrees, and stays convex.

questions.stem: A circular sheet of paper is folded along the lines in the directions shown. The paper, after being punched in the final folded state as shown and unfolded in the reverse order of folding, will look like ________.
questions.figure: A circle with a vertical diameter is folded so the right half goes over onto the left half, giving a half disc on the left. That half disc is folded along its horizontal diameter, the lower half going up onto the upper half, giving a quarter disc whose corner is the centre of the circle. In the final quarter disc, three punches are made: a quarter circle at the corner, a wide rectangle touching the vertical straight edge near its top, and a small square sitting on the horizontal straight edge to the left of the corner. Options show a circle with a small central circle and four rectangles: (A) wide rectangles above and below, small tall rectangles left and right; (B) wide rectangles above and below, small wide rectangles left and right; (C) short wide rectangles above and below, tall rectangles left and right; (D) small tall rectangles above and below, tall rectangles left and right.

diagram.alt: Three stages: disc with vertical fold, half disc with horizontal fold, quarter disc with three punches.

solutionDiagram.alt: Unfolded disc with creases dashed, wide bars above and below the centre, tall rectangles left and right.

options: Wide bars above and below the centre, small tall rectangles left and right
Wide bars above and below the centre, small wide rectangles left and right
Short wide rectangles above and below, tall rectangles left and right
Small tall rectangles above and below, tall rectangles left and right

steps.title: Reflection rule
steps.body: Folding lays one half on the other. A punch through the folded sheet makes a hole in every layer, and unfolding reproduces it by mirror reflection in each crease. If a hole touches or crosses a crease, it joins its mirror image into one larger hole. Rule: unfold in reverse order, reflecting across each crease.

steps.title: Two creases
steps.body: The first fold made the vertical diameter a crease, the second made the horizontal diameter a crease. The quarter disc corner is the centre of the original circle, so the quarter circle punched at the corner unfolds into the full central circle that every option shows.

steps.title: The wide bar on the vertical edge
steps.body: The bar touches the vertical crease and is wide (horizontal). Mirroring across that crease joins it with its twin into one wide bar centred on the vertical diameter. Mirroring across the horizontal crease repeats the pair below the centre. So we get a wide bar above and a wide bar below.

steps.title: The square on the horizontal edge
steps.body: The small square sits on the horizontal crease. Mirroring across it joins the square with its twin into a rectangle twice as tall as wide. Mirroring across the vertical crease repeats it on the other side. So we get a small tall rectangle on the left and on the right.

steps.title: Match
steps.body: Wide bars above and below, small tall rectangles left and right. That is option (A).

shortcut.body: A hole on a crease doubles along the direction across the crease. A horizontal bar on a vertical crease stays horizontal; a square on a horizontal crease turns tall. About 2 minutes.

traps.text: Forgetting that the square on the horizontal crease doubles into a tall shape, and keeping it as a small wide mark.
Swapping the roles of the two creases, putting the tall rectangles above and below and the short bars at the sides.
Turning the wide bar into a small tall mark: reflection across the vertical crease only lengthens the bar sideways.

recognize.clues: A circle folded twice along diameters, three punches in the final quarter piece, and an unfolding in reverse order: each punch is reflected across both creases, and punches that touch a crease merge with their images.
recognize.contrast: Not a single reflection across one axis (ga-spatial.reflection): the two nested creases give each free punch four images, a punch on one crease two, and a punch at the crossing only one.

check.body: Count the holes: the corner punch gives 1 central hole, the bar on the vertical edge gives 2 merged bars after both unfoldings, and the square on the horizontal edge gives 2 merged rectangles. That is 5 holes in total, the central circle with four rectangles, which is the layout every option draws.
